facts.statement: The genus Lesothosaurus was named by paleontologist Peter Galton in 1978.
facts.quote: authority: Galton, 1978

facts.statement: Lesothosaurus lived during the Early Jurassic period.
facts.quote: fossil_range: Early Jurassic,

facts.statement: Fossils of Lesothosaurus have been found in what is now South Africa and Lesotho.
facts.quote: lived during the Early Jurassic in what is now South Africa and Lesotho

facts.statement: Fossils referable to Lesothosaurus may have been known as early as 1959.
facts.quote: Fossils referrable to Lesothosaurus may have been known from as early as 1959

facts.statement: The fossils date to approximately 199 to 190 million years ago.
facts.quote: dating to the Early Jurassic (199(?)-190 million years ago)

facts.statement: Expeditions from 1963 to 1964 recovered many additional fossils of Lesothosaurus.
facts.quote: The holotype was all that was known until expeditions by the London University College to the same site in Lesotho from 1963 to 1964 recovered scores of fossils from Lesothosaurus

facts.statement: Very well-preserved cranial material was described in 1991.
facts.quote: This included very well preserved cranial material, some of the best known, that was described in the 1991

facts.statement: A 2017 study suggested that differences between Stormbergia and Lesothosaurus are likely related to growth.
facts.quote: A study published in 2017 by Baron, Norman & Barrett demonstrated that the differences between Stormbergia and Lesothosaurus are most likely related to the animal's growth

facts.statement: The syntypes were redescribed in 2015 and 2017 using CT technology.
facts.quote: Redescription of the syntypes came in 2015 and 2017, including the integration of CT technology

facts.statement: The only valid species in the genus is Lesothosaurus diagnosticus.
facts.quote: The genus has only one valid species, Lesothosaurus diagnosticus

facts.statement: Lesothosaurus was a lightly built, bipedal animal ranging from 1 to 2 meters in length.
facts.quote: Lesothosaurus was a lightly built, bipedal animal that varied between 1 (3.3 ft) to 2 meters (6.6 ft) long

facts.statement: Lesothosaurus likely was a fast runner due to its long slender legs and slender tail.
facts.quote: Its long slender legs, small arms with hands that would not have been able to grasp properly, and slender tail all suggest that it was a fast runner

facts.statement: Lesothosaurus had a horny, beak-like structure at the tips of its upper and lower jaws.
facts.quote: Like all ornithischians, the tips of Lesothosaurus upper and lower jaws were horny, forming a beaklike structure

facts.statement: Lesothosaurus was likely an opportunistic omnivore that fed primarily on small animals when softer plants were unavailable.
facts.quote: Studies of the tooth wear have shown much less abrasion on the teeth than would be expected of a plant-eater feeding mainly on tough, arid-climate plants, and concluded that Lesothosaurus was probably an opportunistic omnivore, feeding primarily on small animals during seasons when softer plants were not available

facts.statement: Lesothosaurus sliced its food with its beak but could not chew it.
facts.quote: Analysis of its teeth has shown that Lesothosaurus sliced up its food with its beak and was not able to chew its food

facts.statement: Evidence from a 2016 bonebed suggests Lesothosaurus may have lived in groups.
facts.quote: A bonebed of Lesothosaurus described in 2016 includes material from three large individuals. This association suggest that this early ornithischian dinosaur may have lived in groups

facts.statement: It is debated whether Stormbergia is a valid species or a synonym of Lesothosaurus.
facts.quote: The authors argued that Stormbergia is a junior subjective synonym of Lesothosaurus and should be regarded as invalid

facts.statement: The eye sockets of Lesothosaurus were large, accounting for 36% of the skull's basal length.
facts.quote: The orbits are round and large relative to the skull size (making up 36% of the basal skull length i. e. from the premaxilla tip to the posterior margin of the basioccipital).

facts.statement: Lesothosaurus had 15 to 16 tooth positions in its upper jaw, whereas the related Pisanosaurus had only 11 preserved.
facts.quote: There are 15-16 tooth positions in the maxilla, in contrary to the 11 preserved in Pisanosaurus' (a Late Triassic dinosauriform that may be an ornithischian).

facts.statement: Some researchers suggest Lesothosaurus had lips and cheeks based on its neurovascular structure, which resembles that of modern lizards.
facts.quote: The alveolar foramina are on the medial wall of the maxilla and dentary, one per tooth position, and represent the area where the neurovascular supply accesses the dental lamina. This condition is similar to that in the extant Lepidosaurs, which have lizard lips, leading some paleontologists to suggest that Lesothosaurus had cheeks and lips covering its teeth.

facts.statement: The lower jaw of Lesothosaurus had a nearly straight bottom edge with only a slight upward curve at the front tip.
facts.quote: The mandible (lower jaw) of Lesothosaurus has a nearly straight ventral margin and bears only a slight upturn at its anterior tip.

facts.statement: The beak bone at the tip of Lesothosaurus's lower jaw was arrowhead-shaped with a central ridge and side projections.
facts.quote: The predentary is shaped like an arrowhead in ventral view, with one elongated central keel with smaller lateral processes jutting off the sides.

facts.statement: Lesothosaurus possessed two distinct tooth types: long, sharp front teeth and short, robust back teeth.
facts.quote: Lesothosaurus has two types of teeth preserved: long, curved, sharp premaxillary teeth at the front of the mouth; wide, short, robust maxillary and dentary teeth.

facts.statement: Lesothosaurus had a small gap between its front and back teeth, with the last front teeth having small serrations on their edges.
facts.quote: The last two teeth crowns in the series acquire distal and medial denticles. The posterior process of the premaxilla lacks alvelovi, creating a small diastema (gap) in between the premaxillary and maxillary tooth rows.

facts.statement: Evidence of rapid tooth replacement has been found in the back teeth of Lesothosaurus.
facts.quote: This suggests rapid tooth replacement in these teeth.

facts.statement: Unlike the contemporary Heterodontosaurus, Lesothosaurus did not have a distinct slope break on its snout before the eye socket.
facts.quote: The skull lacks a break in slope along the snout anterior to the orbit, as in the contemporary Heterodontosaurus.

facts.statement: Lesothosaurus had only nine cervical vertebrae, though no complete neck series has been preserved.
facts.quote: The cervical (neck) vertebrae were only 9 in number, but no full cervical series are known.

facts.statement: Although no complete back column is known, Lesothosaurus likely possessed between 12 and 15 dorsal vertebrae.
facts.quote: Lesothosaurus has no complete dorsal columns preserved but likely had 12–15 dorsal (back) vertebrae.

facts.statement: The forelimb of Lesothosaurus was significantly shorter than its hindlimb, with the humerus measuring only 63.3% of the femur's length.
facts.quote: The humerus length was only 63.3% as long as the femur length, which is much shorter than other basal ornithischians.

facts.statement: The largest known femur of Lesothosaurus measures 273.70 mm in length.
facts.quote: The largest known femur is from NMQR 3076, which measures 273.70 mm in length.

facts.statement: Lesothosaurus is distinct among its relatives for lacking a fifth metatarsal bone.
facts.quote: Notably, Lesothosaurus lacks a metatarsal V, a distinct trait of the taxon.

facts.statement: The third toe of Lesothosaurus was the longest digit, with a combined length of 57.7 mm.
facts.quote: Digit III was the longest digit by length and had a combined length of 57.7 mm.

facts.statement: Unlike more advanced ornithischians, the toe bones of Lesothosaurus ended in claw-like structures rather than hooves.
facts.quote: The ungual bones of the toes were claw-like, and not hoof-like as in more advanced ornithischians.

facts.statement: A 1991 redescription by Paul Sereno classified Lesothosaurus as a basal member of the order Ornithischia.
facts.quote: However, a 1991 redescription by Paul Sereno suggested that Lesothosaurus and many other "fabrosaurids" were actually basal members of Ornithischia, one of the two main orders of Dinosauria (the other being Saurischia).

facts.statement: Later studies placed Lesothosaurus as the most basal member of Neornithischia, relating it to Agilisaurus, Hexinulsaurus, and Nanosaurus.
facts.quote: Later cladistic studies of basal Ornithischia, which have also found it as the basalmost member of Neornithischia (a group that includes pachycephalosaurs, ceratopsians, and ornithopods) and related to Agilisaurus, Hexinulsaurus, and Nanosaurus.

facts.statement: Some researchers debate whether Lesothosaurus belongs to Neornithischia or is instead an early thyreophoran related to armored dinosaurs.
facts.quote: Alternatively, this dinosaur may be a very early thyreophoran, a member of the group including the armored stegosaurians and ankylosaurians.

facts.statement: Lesothosaurus fossils date to the Lower Jurassic, specifically the Hettangian and Sinemurian ages, approximately 200 to 190 million years ago.
facts.quote: Lesothosaurus is known from fossils found in formations of the Karoo Supergroup, including the Upper Elliot Formation and the Clarens Formation, which date to the Hettangian and Sinemurian ages of the Lower Jurassic, around 200–190 million years ago.

facts.statement: Lesothosaurus was originally misidentified as belonging to the Upper Triassic period before being correctly dated to the Jurassic.
facts.quote: Originally, Lesothosaurus was thought to be from the Upper Triassic period.

facts.statement: Preserved ossified tendons on the back vertebrae suggest Lesothosaurus used them to counteract stress during bipedal movement.
facts.quote: Ossified tendons are preserved attached to the neural spines of anterior dorsals, suggesting they were arranged longitudinally as in Heterodontosaurus, Scelidosaurus, and Hypsilophodon. This feature probably countered stress caused by bending forces acting on the spine during bipedal locomotion.

facts.statement: Researchers suggest that high diversity among heterodontosaurids, including Lesothosaurus, indicates species partitioned food sources to avoid competition.
facts.quote: The high heterodontosaurid diversity have led researchers to conclude that different species might have fed on separate food sources in order to avoid competition (niche partitioning).

facts.statement: Lesothosaurus fossils are found in the red and white sandstones and mudstones of the Upper Elliot and Clarens Formations.
facts.quote: The Upper Elliot Formation consists of red/purple mudstone and red/white sandstone, whereas the slightly younger Clarens Formation consists of white/cream-coloured sandstone.
